system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: information provision and enabling patient behaviors
diagnosis: Chunk-and-check communication for complex medical information
mechanism: Chunk-and-check reduces cognitive load by presenting a small amount of information at a time and confirming comprehension before moving to the next segment. It differs from a single end-of-visit yes/no check because misunderstanding is identified and corrected iteratively.
vignette: A 72-year-old man with newly diagnosed heart failure is learning about daily weights, sodium restriction, three medication changes, and symptoms that should prompt urgent medical attention. After several minutes of explanation, he looks overwhelmed and says, 'That is a lot to remember.' The physician wants to continue teaching while maximizing comprehension.
lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate communication strategy?
correct: Explain one small part of the plan, ask the patient to restate what he will do, clarify errors, and then move to the next part
distractors: Complete the entire explanation first and then ask whether the patient understands
Provide the written instructions and avoid further verbal explanation so the patient is not overloaded
Repeat the complete plan from the beginning using the same wording but more slowly
Ask the patient's family to memorize the plan instead of asking the patient to participate
distractor_notes: A single yes/no check after a long information dump does not implement chunk-and-check and may fail to reveal misunderstanding.
Written material can reinforce learning but does not replace interactive comprehension assessment.
Slower repetition of the same large information block does not reduce cognitive load or verify comprehension segment by segment.
Family support may be useful when desired, but substituting family for an independently participating patient is unnecessary and does not test understanding.
key_expl: Chunk-and-check breaks complex teaching into manageable segments and checks comprehension after each segment, commonly with teach-back. This permits immediate correction before new information is added.
objective: Use chunk-and-check to teach a complex care plan by delivering information in small segments and verifying comprehension after each segment.

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
diagnosis: Patient-engaged warm handoff during an in-practice care transition
mechanism: A warm handoff transfers care face to face between health professionals in front of the patient, treating the patient as a team member who can hear, clarify, correct, and ask questions. This provides a safety check against omissions or distortions during transitions.
vignette: A primary care physician has just evaluated a 58-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes and is transferring her care during the same visit to the clinic pharmacist for intensive medication management. The patient has several questions about which medications she should continue. Both clinicians are available in the clinic.
lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate way to make this transition?
correct: Introduce the pharmacist to the patient and verbally review the clinical problem and plan with both of them present, inviting the patient to correct or clarify information
distractors: Send the pharmacist a brief electronic message after the patient leaves the physician's room
Ask the patient to repeat her entire history to the pharmacist without communication between the clinicians
Transfer the medication list electronically and avoid discussing the plan in front of the patient
Ask a family member to summarize the physician's recommendations to the pharmacist
distractor_notes: An asynchronous message may transmit information but lacks the patient-engaged face-to-face safety check of a warm handoff.
Forcing the patient to reconstruct the history increases burden and risk of omission rather than enabling coordinated communication.
Electronic transfer alone excludes the patient from verification and clarification.
A family member should not replace direct clinician-to-clinician communication and patient participation.
key_expl: A warm handoff occurs face to face between team members in front of the patient and family if present. The patient can hear the exchange, clarify or correct information, and ask questions, making the transition a communication safety check.
objective: Use a patient-engaged warm handoff for an in-practice transition of care when both clinicians are available.

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
diagnosis: Summarizing the patient's narrative and checking whether the summary is accurate
mechanism: An active-listening summary condenses the patient's story and explicitly checks accuracy. It demonstrates attention, exposes misunderstanding, and lets the patient correct the clinician before diagnostic or counseling decisions are made.
vignette: A 46-year-old woman describes intermittent abdominal pain, several dietary changes she has tried, worry that she has cancer, and frustration that previous clinicians focused only on reflux. After listening without interruption, the physician wants to ensure that the patient's priorities and history have been understood correctly before moving to focused questions.
lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next statement?
correct: “Let me make sure I have this right: the pain comes after meals, you have changed your diet, and your biggest concern is cancer. Is there anything I misunderstood or missed?”
distractors: “Your symptoms are most consistent with reflux, so we should focus on that rather than cancer.”
“I understand exactly how you feel; let us move on to the physical examination.”
“Why did you not follow the diet your previous physician recommended?”
“There are many causes of abdominal pain; I will explain all of them before asking more questions.”
distractor_notes: Premature diagnostic reframing does not verify the patient's narrative or priorities.
Claiming complete understanding without checking accuracy is not active-listening verification.
A blaming 'why' question can be judgmental and does not summarize or validate understanding.
An information dump before clarifying the history reverses the appropriate communication sequence.
key_expl: Summarizing key facts and concerns and asking the patient to correct the summary is an active-listening technique. It verifies understanding and signals that the patient's perspective was heard.
objective: Use a concise summary followed by an accuracy check to demonstrate active listening and verify the patient's narrative.

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
diagnosis: Eliciting the patient's explanatory model of illness before counseling
mechanism: Eliciting the patient's explanatory model identifies beliefs about cause, course, consequences, and preferred treatment. This reveals potential discordance between the medical plan and the patient's beliefs and allows counseling to be tailored rather than assuming nonadherence or dismissing beliefs.
vignette: A 50-year-old man with newly diagnosed hypertension says he does not want to start medication because he believes his elevated blood pressure is caused by 'blocked energy' and should be treated with an herbal remedy. He is calm, has decision-making capacity, and is willing to discuss the issue.
lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial response by the physician?
correct: Ask the patient what he thinks is causing the problem, how he believes the herbal remedy will help, and what outcomes he hopes for
distractors: Tell him that his belief is medically incorrect and should not influence treatment decisions
Document medication refusal and end the discussion because he has decision-making capacity
Begin a detailed explanation of hypertension pathophysiology before asking about his beliefs
Ask a family member to persuade him to accept antihypertensive medication
distractor_notes: Dismissal of beliefs can damage trust and misses useful information about the patient's model.
Capacity permits refusal but does not eliminate the clinician's role in respectful exploration and informed counseling.
Counseling before understanding the patient's explanatory model may fail to address the actual concern.
Family persuasion without patient request bypasses direct patient-centered discussion.
key_expl: The clinician should first elicit the patient's explanatory model—beliefs about cause, treatment, and expected outcomes—then provide information and negotiate a plan. AHRQ explicitly recommends eliciting the patient/family explanatory model when educating about diagnosis and medicines.
objective: Elicit a patient's explanatory model before attempting to reconcile health beliefs with an evidence-based treatment plan.

system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
diagnosis: Asking the patient how they want a family companion involved in the visit
mechanism: Family involvement should be guided by the patient's preferences when the patient has capacity. The clinician should preserve patient participation and privacy while allowing supportive family involvement to the extent the patient desires.
vignette: A 61-year-old woman with newly diagnosed breast cancer comes to an oncology visit with her adult daughter. The patient has full decision-making capacity. Her daughter immediately begins answering questions and asks the physician to discuss all treatment details with her because she 'handles medical things for Mom.' The patient's own preference for her daughter's involvement has not yet been established.
lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
correct: Ask the patient directly how she would like her daughter to participate in the discussion and decision making
distractors: Continue speaking primarily with the daughter because she appears more comfortable with medical information
Exclude the daughter from the room for the entire visit without first asking the patient
Ask the daughter to decide how much information the patient should receive
Require the patient to sign a durable power of attorney before the daughter can remain in the room
distractor_notes: A capable patient remains the central participant; a companion should not dominate by default.
Private time can be important, but complete exclusion without eliciting the patient's wishes is unnecessarily paternalistic.
The daughter cannot control disclosure to a capable patient unless the patient has specifically authorized an arrangement consistent with her preferences.
A legal surrogate designation is not required merely for a patient-selected support person to participate in a visit.
key_expl: The physician should establish the capable patient's preference for family involvement. Family can be helpful, but the focus should remain on the patient and participation should reflect the patient's wishes.
objective: Preserve patient autonomy by asking a capable patient how they want a family companion involved before assigning the companion a role in communication or decisions.
